lesson.title: From Slopes to Lines: Why Chemists Integrate Rate Laws
lesson.summary: An integrated rate law rewrites a rate law as an equation for concentration as a function of time, letting chemists predict how much reactant remains at any moment and use straight-line graphs to confirm reaction order from real data.
lesson.body:
Every rate law discussed so far, rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, is a differential rate law: it tells you the rate at a given instant based on the concentrations present at that instant. That is extremely useful for comparing reaction speeds and for determining reaction order through the method of initial rates, but it does not directly answer a question chemists ask constantly: how much reactant will be left after 10 minutes? Or, how long will it take for half the reactant to be consumed? Answering those questions requires an equation for concentration as a function of time, [A] as a function of t, rather than an equation for rate as a function of concentration. That kind of equation is called an integrated rate law.

The connection between the two is calculus: since rate is defined as -d[A]/dt (the instantaneous rate of change of concentration with time, with a sign flip so rate comes out positive for a disappearing reactant, exactly the instantaneous rate idea from earlier in this unit), setting that equal to the rate law and integrating over time turns a rate equation into a concentration-versus-time equation. You do not need to carry out that integration yourself to use the results, but it is worth knowing where the formulas below come from: they are simply the rate law, worked forward through time.

Each reaction order produces a different integrated rate law, and, remarkably, each one becomes a straight line when you plot the right transformation of concentration against time. For a zero order reaction, [A] itself plotted against t is a straight line, with the form [A] = [A]0 - kt. For a first order reaction, the natural logarithm of [A] plotted against t is a straight line, with the form ln[A] = ln[A]0 - kt. For a second order reaction, the reciprocal of [A] plotted against t is a straight line, with the form 1/[A] = 1/[A]0 + kt.

This is where the graphing skills built earlier pay off directly: instead of guessing a reaction's order, a chemist can take a single series of concentration-versus-time measurements and make three different plots, [A] versus t, ln[A] versus t, and 1/[A] versus t. Whichever of the three comes out as a straight line reveals the reaction order, and the slope of that line hands you the rate constant k as well (with a sign that depends on which form you used). This graphical approach is one of the most reliable ways to confirm reaction order from real experimental data, since a genuinely linear plot is hard to fake and easy to check by eye. The next chapter works through the zero order case in complete, worked-out detail, since it is the most direct starting point of the three.
